In simulations of numerical relativity, initial data requirements pose a significant obstacle, particularly for complex systems involving spinning objects in gravitational waves. A novel method we call the "Complexity-Termination Threshold for Gauge" (CTTG) or simply "Complexity Termination" (CT) strategy, which limits the complexity of a gauge function rather than the total volume, provides a solution to this challenge. Using an algebraic gauge selection in 3D space, we have achieved successful extraction of gravitational waves for spinning binary mergers, even in cases where conventional methods fail due to gauge instability. This approach has been successfully applied to a range of scenarios, including a perturbative analysis of the binary merger process and a non-perturbative simulation of a black hole surrounded by matter. Compared to conventional methods, the CTTG technique allows for a much finer resolution of physical parameters, as demonstrated by a detailed analysis of a binary merger simulation. This technique has the potential to advance our understanding of complex astrophysical events involving spinning objects, and its applications extend to other areas of numerical relativity, such as black hole formation in scalar field systems. A software package called "geum" containing the complexity-termination strategy, as well as other useful tools for solving the Hamiltonian constraint, is available for public use. This approach can also be used in 2D space, which may have implications for the study of gravitational waves in compact binary mergers. This research was conducted as part of the projects "Numerical Relativity without a Numerical Relativity Budget," and "Compact Binary Merger Observables in Full Non-Linear General Relativity." The development of the complexity-termination strategy has been aided by computational resources provided by the Texas Advanced Computing Center. Understanding how the brain controls different gait patterns is crucial for developing effective treatments for various neurological disorders and injuries that affect mobility. Recent studies using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and electroencephalography (EEG) have identified the brain regions active during ambulation, but the precise state of the brain during different gait elements such as stepping and standing remains unclear. To address this knowledge gap, researchers recorded the electrical activity of the brain through electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings in animals while they walked on a treadmill, and then analyzed the data to determine the frequency patterns associated with stepping and standing. Unlike previous findings using fMRI and EEG, the ECoG recordings revealed distinct frequency patterns associated with stepping vs standing, and demonstrated that the brain's state changes continuously throughout gait cycles. Furthermore, the research showed that the frequencies associated with gait change patterns, and that walking is maintained by the interaction of multiple frequency patterns. The novel insights gained from this study using ECoG recordings in animals could be applied to humans, and may contribute to the development of prosthetic devices that can restore mobility in individuals with mobility disorders. The research also highlights the importance of considering the complex state of the brain during gait, and the possibility of developing more effective treatments for various mobility disorders, such as Parkinson's disease, by targeting specific frequency patterns associated with gait. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to detecting temporal changes in connectivity using a combination of recurrent neural networks, accompanied by an optimization procedure to compute an optimal threshold for connection detection. Unlike existing solutions, our method is capable of extracting time-dependent connections from short data sequences, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments on synthetic and real-world data. Specifically, we apply our technique to analyze the connectivity of a well-known benchmark in neuroscience, the Henneberg circuit, as well as two real-world systems: a set of stock prices and the global temperature patterns over the past 1000 years. Our findings show that connections can vary significantly over time, and we highlight the significance of considering these temporal changes when researching complex systems. The code for this project is available at this link https://github.com/AbdulTahaDaud/DeepDynamicalGraphs.

Animals play a significant role in raising awareness about conservation efforts and understanding various biological processes.  Unmilling, a researcher in ecology, often uses field observations to collect data on areas where certain species inhabit.  This research helps scientists identify patterns of migration, defense mechanisms against predators, and other essential behaviors of different species.  Due to the importance of this information, detecting movement in videos of biological samples is now a pressing need.  This paper introduces a novel approach to automatically identify movement within biological videos while ignoring stagnant elements of the sample.  The proposed method involves distinguishing moving parts from the background and separating components that are attached to the sample but move independently.  This is achieved through a computational technique that detects and tracks elements exhibiting independent motion.  This method has been applied to various types of samples, including plants and animals, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness.  The code for this research has been made public and is available online.  This paper also highlights some potential conservation-related applications of this finding.  One such example is detecting the presence of insects that carry diseases by identifying movement in videos of certain plants.  This in turn can help develop more efficient monitoring systems for detecting these insects.  This has significant implications for preventing the spread of certain plant diseases and reducing economic losses resulting from them.  This has already been implemented on a large scale in some rice fields in Japan.  This paper also presents a novel approach to detecting movement based on the concept of "structural independent components".  This approach involves separating the different components of a sample based on the level of freedom they possess.  This is a groundbreaking idea in computer vision that can be applied to various scenarios beyond biological videos.  This approach can be used to develop more sophisticated models for predicting the behavior of complex systems. Contextual decision-making is a challenging task that involves selecting actions based on context, and it has various applications in contextual Markov decision processes, contextual linear gambits, and personalized recommendations. This research explores a collaborative version of contextual linear gambits, where multiple agents aim to optimize actions in different contexts, and it is assumed that the context-action weights and noise variance are shared across the agents. We develop an efficient and decentralized learning method using the Frank-Wolfe algorithm to estimate the shared parameters and determine the optimal action at each context. Our theoretical findings include a regret bound of $O(\sqrt{T}\log(T)})$ for a fixed context distribution and a minimax regret of $O(\sqrt{H_T}\log(H_T))$ for a time-varying context distribution. Our results also show that our approach is optimal for a fixed context distribution by comparing it with a decentralized version of the empirical risk minimizer. Our algorithm's efficiency and effectiveness are further demonstrated through simulated experiments. Our code is available at https://github.com/AlexKouhkal/contextual-gambit-learning. This research was presented at the 52nd Annual Conference on Information Systems and Technology for Education, and it has been previously published in the proceedings.

This research focuses on advancing the design of a monopod for hopping on soft, uneven ground by conducting numerical analysis and physical experiments to evaluate and improve the robot's design. Initially, a computational model was developed to simulate the interaction between the robot and a soft surface using the finite element method, which was effective in assessing the impact and subsequent hopping phases. However, it failed to accurately replicate the formation of fissures in the ground. To address this limitation, a alternative computational model was developed using the discrete element method, which provided a more precise representation of the ground interaction. This method also enabled the reduction of friction between ground elements and the robot's foot, facilitating the formation of fissures in the simulation. To enhance the design of the monopod, recommendations were made based on the results of the simulations, which were subsequently physically tested to validate the proposed design improvements. The developed robot was capable of safely hopping on soft surfaces with varying levels of hardness and uneven terrain, demonstrating a high level of stability and reliability. The research was conducted in close collaboration with the robotics group at Columbia University. The simulation tools and model, as well as the designed and tested robot, are available for public use. The development of the monopod was funded by the NASA Robotics Engineering Emeritus Program. The associated costs were approximately $200,000 over a period of three years. The research was focused on developing a hopping gait for the monopod, which has also been found suitable for other terrains including soft rocky ground, soil, and snow. Our study examines the impact of electron-electron interactions on the electronic properties of an infinite-layer nickelate, focusing on this material's intriguing similarities to cuprates and ferrochalcogens. We develop a dual-band model to represent the energy spectra, incorporating screening effects from nearby electrons on the site fidelity and exchange integrals. Our calculations reveal the emergence of heavy electrons in a half-filled middle-band, with a localized moment and adjacent charge and spin instability. However, when the middle-band is partially filled, our results show that the screening of the on-site interaction by nearby electrons leads to an absence of static moment formation and instead results in a heavy Fermi liquid phase, closely related to the ferrochalcogen material family. Our dual-band model allows for varying band filling and provides a means to experimentally map our predictions to actual energy spectra through angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper addresses that challenge by introducing a new technique to enhance semi-supervised image segmentation. The proposed method involves training a network with two outputs: one for segmentation and one for classification, using only summaries of annotated data. These network outputs must conform to the same distribution, which is ensured using a proposed regularization technique called consistency regularization. This technique simplifies the challenge of balancing classification and segmentation tasks, while allowing the network to learn from partially annotated images. We evaluate and analyze two versions of the proposed technique, along with a conventional transfer learning approach, using MRI brain segmentation tasks. The results show that the proposed technique outperforms standard approaches, especially when the amount of annotated data is limited. The code for this project is available online at https://github.com/ghrasoul/Consistency-Regression-Semi-Supervised-Segmentation.

Nonetheless, even with current implementations like Z3 and CVC4, there are still obstacles to incorporating automatic proof production on a broad scale. We derive equations describing these objects' dynamics and thermodynamics, using a multi-fluid relativistic thermodynamics framework. We then apply these findings to analyze static, spherically symmetric objects and rotating black holes in the context of nonisotropic dual-fluids. Our study reveals that such objects can exist, both with and without a boundary, and that their properties depend on the interaction between the two fluids and the level of nonisotropy exhibited by one of the fluids. We also find that the phenomenon of nonisotropy is more pronounced in black holes than in stellar objects, primarily due to the powerful gravitational pull of these rotating black holes. Our research builds upon previous studies of self-gravitating objects composed of multiple fluids and provides a more comprehensive understanding of these complex systems. Our results agree with the existing literature and provide novel insights into the behavior of nonisotropic dual-fluids, as well as the properties of black holes and rotating stars. Our analysis also facilitates the utilization of nonisotropic dual-fluids in models of compact stars and walking first-order phase transitions. Most current sequence-to-sequence based grammatical error rectification models rely on vast amounts of data for high-quality results. However, correcting grammatical errors in languages like Arabic, Hebrew and Persian requires significant resources and a significant amount of time due to issues like text anonymization and extensive data availability. In response to this challenge, this paper introduces a domain transfer approach that enables the efficient training of EGR models on just three examples from new domains without the need for vast amounts of data. The resulting model achieves a 1.85 improvement in exact match score on the IELTS NSE for Persian when compared to a trained model from scratch. Additionally, our approach surpasses previously reported scores on the IELTS NSE for Arabic and achieves a score of 80.58 on the NSE for Hebrew. Our code has been made publicly available at github.com/s0mew1nder/grammer_metareader.

It is known that finding an equitable allocation that benefits all agents, using the most liberal pricing system available, is possible when there are two agents present. However, when the number of agents exceeds two, the possibility of an equitable allocation existing in a general setting is not well understood. In our current research, we focus on a specific scenario with three agents and prove the existence of a equitable allocation that is also a pure Nash Equilibrium in a first-price auction system. Moreover, we achieve this result while ensuring that the benefits derived from this equilibrium are maximal. Our primary contribution thus falls within the category of recent results examining the interconnection between agent-centric and multiagent reasoning, specifically where the agent behavior can be modeled using a self-centered and noncooperative approach. In the process of achieving this result, we develop a new characterization of high-demand pure Nash Equilibria, which may be useful in its own right. Additionally, our current research offers a bound of sorts on the overall social value captured by a pure Nash Equilibrium in a specific setting. This further may have utility as a standalone result in its own right. We consider a particular scenario with three agents and prove that the sum of the values obtained by each agent at the equilibrium is limited to a factor of 27 times the maximum possible value, which can be achieved when all agents value a particular item at the same level of intensity. A numerical model of disk evolution indicates that this observed configuration can result from the gravitational influence of a lone giant planet. A subsequent search for the planet itself using the Hubble Space Telescope and ground-based spectroscopic data revealed a gas giant with a mass similar to that of Jupiter and an orbital path consistent with the predicted pattern. Further analysis of the system, using both observations and simulations, reveals a notable lack of high-energy stellar activity, unlike expectations based on similar systems. This unusual behavior may be caused by the alignment of the planet's magnetic field with roughly 5 degrees of the stellar axis, reducing coronal interaction and resulting in the observed low activity levels. This unique system provides valuable insights for researchers studying the relationship between high-energy stellar activity, planetary systems, and the orientation of galaxies. Additionally, the analysis of spectral data for UGC 8839 reveals an anomalous absorption pattern in the far red region of the spectral range, followed by another pattern in the ultraviolet region, which may be associated with a massive outflow of gas and dust from the system over its lifetime. Moreover, this system shares a similar orientation with an adjacent galaxy subgroup, suggesting that the galactic poles may play a significant role in shaping the planetary systems within it. Lastly, this research was made possible by the availability of high-resolution Hubble Space Telescope data, and the findings highlight the capabilities of the Hubble Space Telescope in discovering planetary systems similar to UGC 8839.

The notion of single-particle entanglement is often misinterpreted, as it can be seen as a variation of the EPR paradox, where two particles are physically separated and share an entangled state. Single-particle entanglement refers to a situation where a system consists of two parts, one of which involves a single particle with an entangled state. This state of affairs is often mistakenly linked to single-particle entanglement. However, when an external parameter is modified, the state of the single particle remains unchanged, indicating no genuine nonlocal effect. In contrast, a genuine nonlocal impact would be reflected in a change in the single-particle state. Specifically, we show that in a scenario involving two parties, where one has control over an external parameter, single-particle entanglement is required for particle steering. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 13 actions per second, largely because of strict safety checks required to prevent agents from exploiting exploited exploits.

TextWorldExpress surpasses previous texts-based games in speed while maintaining comparable difficulty levels, as evidenced by the minimal decline in performance by state-of-the-art texts-based agents when playing at higher speeds.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence classification models, research suggests that incorporating information about the semantic relationships between sentences can lead to better performance. However, incorporating this information requires a manual process by language experts to define the relations between sentences, which is both time-consuming and difficult to scale. To address this challenge, we present an automatic method called DiscSense for identifying the semantic relationships between sentences that are connected by discourse indicators. This method uses a combination of supervised machine learning and linguistic analysis to classify discourse indicators into different categories and determine the nature of the relationships they indicate. We evaluated this method on multiple datasets and found that DiscSense leads to improved performance of sentence classification models, especially when the models are challenged with subtle semantic differences between sentences. To further demonstrate the value of DiscSense, we showed that incorporating this method into the training process of sentence classification models highlights areas where they struggle with certain discourse indicators and sentences that contain these indicators. We also made DiscSense available as an open-source tool for the research community. In addition, we provided a dataset of annotated sentences that were classified using DiscSense and reviewed the findings of this study in the context of existing research on discourse indicators and semantic similarity between sentences. To the best of our knowledge, DiscSense is the first automatic method for identifying the semantic relationships between sentences that are connected by discourse indicators, and we believe that this method can be used in other applications that involve the analysis of discourse indicators and sentence relationships. We explored one such application in this study, namely using DiscSense to annotate the discourse indicators that express contradiction, but we believe that this method can be used to annotate other relationships as well. We made a dataset of annotated sentences that were classified using DiscSense available to the research community, and we hope that this dataset and DiscSense will be useful for developing more effective sentence classification models, especially those that challenge the current state-of-the-art model, BERT. To develop more challenging models, we proposed a method that identifies areas where the models struggle with certain discourse indicators and suggests possible improvements for building these models, including adding more challenges in the form of sentences that contain the discourse indicators that express contradiction, and incorporating the annotations of these indicators into the training process of the models. We also discussed the implications of this study for the research on the theories of discourse connections and semantic relationships between sentences. We investigate the landscape of a particular matrix optimization problem, aiming to minimize the matrix norm under a non-convex constraint on the matrix factors. Using a Riemannian perspective, we establish that the problem's landscape is geodesically convex, implying that along an arbitrary direction on the manifold, the quadratic Taylor series expansion of the function is positive definite. This convexity property holds everywhere, and we demonstrate its connection to a specific version of the classical AM-GM inequality. Furthermore, we find that the optimization problem's solution set is contained in the level set defined by the negative eigenvalue of the Riemannian Hessian being zero, which is a more stringent condition. This more stringent condition enables us to characterize the optimization problem's solutions, showing that they correspond to the rank-k matrix whose diagonal entries are equal to one, and all off-diagonal entries are zero. In the case of matrix factorization, this means that the optimization problem is to minimize the matrix norm under the constraint that the matrix entries are bounded by one, with the number of constraints equal to the matrix rank. We also examine the optimization problem's local geometry, revealing that the Riemannian Hessian has at least one nonzero eigenvalue at any critical point. This information allows us to classify the critical points found through the gradient descent method. We provide empirical evidence for the geodesic convexity near the global optimum achieved using the gradient descent method. Lastly, we discuss the relationship between this convex landscape and the available numerical methods, highlighting that the geodesic convexity ensures global convergence of the gradient descent method, while the Riemannian Hessian's spectral properties guarantee the stability of the blocking numerical method. We also examine the optimization problem's explicit solutions for a range of matrix functions, as well as the convex landscape properties for a related matrix optimization problem under the trace norm. We provide a preliminary analysis of the geodesic convex landscape for the related matrix optimization problem under the Schur concave norm, showcasing that the corresponding level sets are geodesically convex. However, this analysis is not as comprehensive as that performed for the matrix optimization problem under the matrix norm, and we leave a more detailed examination for future work. Notably, this finding also circumvents another unsolved problem that asked for all non-bipartite cubic graphs to be edge-tintable using three colors within the context of the "Filling" method. We investigated a range of coevolutionary genetic strategies in a symmetric Cournot model, focusing on the interaction between players with different learning preferences and varying levels of sensitivity to innovation. Our findings showed that the convergence to a Nash equilibrium is challenging and often impossible in static Cournot models, with players who take risks and those who adopt a collaborative approach converging to different equilibrium points. In contrast, dynamic models exhibited greater flexibility, allowing players with different learning styles to occupy distinct equilibrium states based on their level of innovation sensitivity. Notably, a model featuring coevolution at a 1:1 ratio achieved stability at a Nash equilibrium, even with noisy conditions. Moreover, a shift from a 1:1 to a 10:1 ratio led to the establishment of a regime with reduced innovation, resulting in the players settling at the pre-noise Nash equilibrium. These outcomes highlight the importance of considering the complexity of human learning in economic models and the potential benefits of a 1:1 coevolutionary model, which can provide a framework for social cooperation that is similar to the manner in which immune systems promote diversity as a vital component of evolution. Our research also demonstrated that the 1:1 coevolutionary model can be an effective means of reducing noise and acceleration, which is analogous to the manner in which immune systems in biological populations eliminate pathogens and accelerate evolution. Our results further showed that the composition of a population made up of different learning preferences can change over time in response to changes in conditions, a capability that we refer to as "evolutionary memory." This capability is similar to the manner in which genetic memory works, and it allows the population to change smoothly in response to sudden changes, which is similar to the response of biological populations to genetic mutations. Our research involved a wide range of simulations, as well as a mathematical analysis of the stability of the population made up of different learning preferences, which provided a comprehensive understanding of the complex dynamics of the 1:1 coevolutionary model. This understanding is crucial for improving the model, which can be achieved through a mathematical analysis of the desired level of cooperation, combined with an adjustment of the parameters of the model, including the level of innovation, the level of noise, and the time period over which the population makes decisions. Our research involved a simulation of a wide range of conditions, which can be applied to a wide range of economic and biological contexts, which are characterized by complex interactions between different elements and components. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have gained widespread acceptance for various image classification tasks. Despite their success, CNNs are prone to performance degradation under certain environmental conditions, such as temperature fluctuations and aging effects, which cause faults in hardware. To address this issue, research has focused on validating that CNNs can withstand these faults, with some work establishing a basis for the tolerance of CNNs to image compression and mask attacks. However, a definitive security case validating CNNs' resilience against faults has yet to be established. In the present study, we provide preliminary evidence for a security case, demonstrating that CNNs are resistant to faults caused by activation interval clipping. Activation interval clipping is a straightforward, efficient technique that involves limiting the input data to a specified range, and our findings show that this technique is effective in withstanding faults, especially when it results in activation interval distortion. Our research involves distorting the activation intervals of a ResNet-200 model trained for CIFAR-100, and our results show that it can tolerate a range of faults, including those caused by various activation interval shapes and sizes, and that it can withstand a particular hardware fault scenario. When applying this technique to a MNIST model trained for EMNIST classification, our findings show that it can tolerate a different kind of fault, i.e., those caused by compress-queue, and that it can withstand a range of compress-queue values, from 8 to 32. Our approach provides a practical means of making CNNs more robust with minimal additional costs, and it paves the way for establishing a security case for CNNs' resilience against faults in a wider context. Our code is available at: https://github.com/ghassan-k/activation-interval-supervision.

Multilingual modeling has been a growing area of interest, aiming to integrate knowledge across multiple languages to enhance the performance of various natural language processing tasks. We explore multi-lingual shared semantic space construction, which assumes multiple language datasets are embedded in a single space while preserving their individual characteristics. Building on this assumption, we devise a novel approach to represent words across multiple languages in a single space by utilizing a cluster-consistent neural network. This model ensures that the representation of words respects their internal structures and patterns within each language. We further develop a multi-learning framework that leverages multi-lingual shared semantic spaces to improve performance on multiple tasks. Our approach delivers superior results compared to state-of-the-art methods in various evaluations. The code is available at https://github.com/lingua-terra/msssc.

This paper presents an examination of mid-rapidity particle production for Xe-Xe collisions at a nucleon-nucleon collision energy of 5.44 TeV, across a wide range of transverse momenta. Newly available data from the ALICE experiment at the CERN LHC facilitate this study, which covers ten different particle species - pions, kaons, protons, and photons - based on combined charge and magnitude measurements. Observed trends show that the ratio of particle yields to entropy remains steady across various collision energies and is unaffected by the centrality of collisions. Furthermore, the magnitude of particle yields during Xe-Xe collisions at this energy level is found to be between those observed for lead-lead collisions at 5.02 TeV and those for proton-proton collisions at 7 TeV, with ratios determined for different centrality intervals. Overall, our research reinforces the long-established rule that particle production ratios are influenced by the colliding particles' mass rather than the energy of the collision, and provides unique insights into particle production within the most central collisions. Additionally, we compare our findings to existing data from the ALICE experiment, the STAR experiment at RHIC, and the CMS experiment at the LHC, and offer predictions for future Ouroboros Xe-Xe collisions. In December 2019, a violent pandemic-related explosion occurred in Chile, following the onset of worldwide COVID-19 transmission. This social unrest spread rapidly across the country and its regions, exceeding expectations based on traditional epidemiological models of contagion. To explain this rapid dissemination, we propose a novel mathematical framework that combines epidemiological and social transmission principles. Based on this model, we were able to simulate the start of the unrest in Chile and the surrounding area, using the nearby Latin American region as our natural barrier. Our simulation revealed that the rate of unrest transmission per unit distance between adjacent regions can be estimated at approximately 0.5, which is remarkably similar to the 0.5 to 0.6 estimated rate of COVID-19 transmission in the same area. To further validate our model, we simulated the decline in unrest cases in Santiago, which corresponded to the projected course of COVID-19 transmission with the same model parameters. Ultimately, our analysis suggests that the explosion of unrest in Chile can be understood through the lens of epidemiological transmission theory, specifically in relation to COVID-19 transmission. This analysis highlights the significance of identifying and managing transmission hotspots, as well as the critical role of middle-level administration in addressing local issues that could contribute to the breakdown of public order. This model has the potential to be applied to similar situations in other countries. The associated computer code is available online at https://github.com/ghik/epidemiology_chile. This research develops an innovative method for addressing the satisfiability issue with a particular type of regular expression known as Regular Expression Inequalities (REIs). Unlike traditional regular expressions, REIs exclude the union operation and are instead characterized by inequalities of the form $x \subseteq y$, where $x$ and $y$ are regular expressions. Our primary contribution is a sound and complete procedure to determine whether a given set of REIs is satisfiable using a specific set of characters, based on a combination of the traditional Brzozowski regular expression builder backwards ward approach. Additionally, REIs can be translated into regular expression inclusion problems, offering a means to utilize existing solutions for regular expression inclusion within the realm of REIs. However, our research demonstrates that the problem of determining whether a given set of REIs is satisfiable using a given set of characters is, in fact, equivalent in complexity to the problem of determining whether a given regular language is empty, which is known to be at least as complex as the problem of deciding whether a context-free grammar is empty, a problem renowned for its high level of complexity. Mobile agents require accurate navigation, and VIO techniques can provide this by combining visual and inertial data. However, training and applying these models come with several challenges, including the need for a large amount of initial data for model training and the presence of drift occurring over time. To address these issues, we developed the EMA-VIO model, which utilizes an external memory attention mechanism to adapt to changing environments. By updating only a subset of the model's parameters, we minimize the need for continuous retraining. In addition, the model's internal clock learns to ignore noisy inertial measurements by incorporating a regularization term into its objective function. We evaluated the EMA-VIO model on datasets from real experiments and simulated scenarios, and the results show its superiority over comparable models. The model was also applied to a critical real-world application, air-ground collaborative navigation, where it outperformed the state-of-the-art method. The code is available online at https://github.com/ShangYueXu/EMA-VIO.

This paper proposes a new framework called Federated Selective Integration (FSI) to address the challenges of disparate data formats and quality in federated learning. The framework emphasizes a collaborative approach among institutions to determine the most trustworthy data points and combine only those with confidence. We introduce novel methods for adaptive detection of reliable and inconsistent data, and propose three combination strategies with different weight assignments to cater to diverse scenario requirements. The proposed approaches are evaluated using real-world datasets from multiple sources, and the results show significant improvements in performance compared to existing techniques. Furthermore, FSI demonstrates high potential for application in sensitive and large-scale federated settings. We explore two scenarios of data quality validation, including threshold-based and anomaly-based methods, and show that FSI delivers outstanding results in various evaluation metrics. The code for the proposed methods is available at https://github.com/lingwei0811/FSI.

Previously, studies have examined the rank growth in fields with specific properties, such as being generated by the x-coordinates of rational points on a particular curve or being generated by Kummer extensions. In this work, we derive explicit formulas for the rank growth in $Q(\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3})$ and $Q(\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{5})$, and provide computational evidence for the rank growth in $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions. Furthermore, we discuss the potential connections between the rank growth and particular x-coordinates of rational points on an elliptic curve, or the rank growth and specific Kummer extensions, such as $Q(\sqrt{3}, \sqrt{5})$. In this latter case, we observe that the rank growth is associated with the 2-torsion points on an elliptic curve, and the associated overcounting factor can be expressed in terms of the Frobenius automorphism and the Galois group of the quartic extension. In the case of $S_4$ quartic extensions, we find that the rank growth is associated with the rank growth in two distinct Kummer extensions, resulting in a twice-as-fast rank growth compared to the rank growth in a single Kummer extension. We're investigating the quantum thermodynamics of holographic systems using the quasilocal operator quantum error correction framework. This foundation enables a focus on the relationships between particular operators rather than the entire CFT. It leads to a discussion of holographic geometries in the context of the trivalent vertex, resulting in the identification of a specific geodesic in the holographic state. Our analysis reveals that this geodesic possesses properties similar to those of a radial curve, which are typically considered indicative of a specific holographic boundary, although it's theoretically possible for other geometries to exhibit these properties. Furthermore, by comparing the areas of the boundary to the von Neumann entropy of the system, we find that they remain proportional during the process of entanglement growth. This proportionality is essential for maintaining the validity of the quantum null energy condition, which is a fundamental principle in quantum thermodynamics. Additionally, we determine the bound on the change in entropy during this process, which is directly related to the curvature of the geodesic and system boundary. These results are particularly relevant to the Little Hierarchy Problem in the Standard Model and the hierarchy problem in asymptotically free theories, as they demonstrate that the hierarchy between the large and small distances is necessary for allowing the system to access a specific, desirable infrared asymptotic regime following a scattering process. The model also predicts distinct planetary evolution paths based on specific disk conditions, leading to feedback loops that influence disk evolution and the formation of planetary systems. We present DynaSOAr, a parallel memory allocator tailored for object-oriented programming on GPUs. By introducing a novel "allocation region" concept, DynaSOAr optimizes memory usage and reduces fragmentation. A concurrent approach is taken to allocate memory, both globally and locally, to accommodate various use cases, including multi-threaded applications. To accommodate different data formats, DynaSOAr features a "type agnosticism" feature, allowing a single, versatile allocator to handle diverse applications. To further increase efficiency, DynaSOAr includes a "re-allocation" mechanism to efficiently reallocate memory, reducing the time and effort associated with re-allocating memory. To validate DynaSOAr's effectiveness, we compare it to the official NVIDIA memory allocator, NVMALLOC, across a range of benchmarks, demonstrating DynaSOAr's superior performance in terms of execution time and memory usage. To ensure ease of integration, we provide simple examples of DynaSOAr's API usage in both CUDA and OpenCL. DynaSOAr's superior performance, coupled with its easy integration, makes it an ideal choice for object-oriented programming on GPUs, particularly in fields where memory allocation accounts for a significant portion of computation time. We put DynaSOAr through testing across a range of applications, including physics simulations, machine learning, and visualization tools, demonstrating DynaSOAr's broad utility. To facilitate further development and customization, we provide DynaSOAr's source code as a standalone, open-source project.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model, applicable to all impurity states, incorporates the effects of hybridization, localization, and spin-orbit interaction. It has been successfully integrated with a general method for analyzing the local spectra of complex systems and has been applied to calculate the energies of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states for both individual Mn atoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface. The results show that this approach accurately describes the shift from a double well state to a bond-induced state as the distance between the Mn dimers changes. Furthermore, this model has been utilized to interpret experimental findings obtained using tunneling spectroscopy for both individual Mn atoms and Mn dimers, demonstrating a clear agreement between the theoretical and experimental results. The developed framework has been found to be particularly effective in providing a clear understanding of the effects caused by the asymmetry of the superconducting gap and the spin-orbit interaction on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states. The presence of the Kondo resonance in the spectra has been predicted and the possibility of its observation discussed. The developed theory has been applied to a range of situations and its capabilities have been demonstrated. It has also been demonstrated that the average magnetic moment can be related to the position and width of the YSR states, however, this relationship depends on the specific system under investigation. The developed framework has further been utilized to interpret the results for Mn dimers located at equivalent sites on the Ni(111) surface, showing that the opening of the YSR gap as far down as 10K is possible. The developed theoretical approach has been compared with an alternative method of analyzing the local spectra of complex systems and has been found to be equivalent to it. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO$_{2}$ using a quantum-kernel hybrid DFT method.  To account for the effects of static and dynamic correlations, the study incorporated a combination of pure and screened DFT-based interactions.  Our research examined a range of configurations for both carbon and nitrogen defects, analyzing their electronic and magnetic arrangements in order to determine the prevalence of magnetic properties.  Our findings indicated that carbon defects exhibited spin polarization in about 20% of cases, typically associated with magnetic moments of 6$\autocap{f}$u, and often linked to specific atomic configurations such as the presence of double bonds between the carbon and neighboring oxygen atoms, or the alignment of their $p$ orbital pairs.  In contrast, nitrogen defects displayed spin polarization in around 30% of cases, primarily related to the alignment of $p$ orbital pairs or the formation of a double bond between the nitrogen and neighboring oxygen atoms, both of these scenarios being more prevalent when nitrogen is bonded to silicon impurities.  Our study also analyzed the possible occurrence of static and dynamic correlations alone, which revealed that static correlations alone cannot explain the magnitude of the magnetic moments, whereas dynamic correlations alone can, although they are overestimated in some cases.  However, the combination of both static and dynamic correlations provided a more accurate explanation for the magnitude of the magnetic moments. The origin of the elastic production of top quarks remains an unresolved mystery in the Standard Model. To delve deeper into this enigma, a new search strategy is proposed that aims to discover the elastic production of top-quark pairs in proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. The proposed method involves analyzing forward-scattered protons by capturing elastic scattering data with a silicon tracker and a highly sensitive Roman pot detector. The use of leading protons with low energy allows for the incorporation of precise information on proton momentum, which enhances the elastic top-quark production signal while minimizing background. The predicted suppression of the forward proton momentum distribution of the elastic top-quark pair signal by Lorentz transformation effects further enhances the search's sensitivity. The proposed method has the potential to discover elastic top-quark pair production with data from the Large Hadron Collider's 13-TeV run, with a predicted cross-section sensitivity of approximately 0.88 fb-1. Furthermore, this search strategy is highly versatile and can be adapted for use with upcoming and future high-energy colliders, such as the Future Circular Collider, which is expected to yield discoveries at cross-section values as low as 0.25 fb-1. The proposed method of studying the LHC data with a silicon tracker and Roman pot detectors at the forward endoscope provides a promising approach for uncovering the elastic generation of top quarks and demonstrates the effectiveness of this technique for detecting this process at a much later date, far beyond the LHC era. The non-equilibrium quantum dynamics of a qutrit lattice model, mimicking massive scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in (1+1)D, is investigated in this study. By applying a variety of quantum perturbation techniques to initial Gaussian states, we observe multiple distinct effects: the emergence of a convenient reference frame through amplitude scaling; the identification of critical points based on perturbed conformal field theory; and the relevance of trapped ions to this model. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive evaluation of a proposal for a quantum simulator involving qutrits, assessing the condition under which the number of effective qudit dimensions remains sufficiently large to ensure reliable simulation accuracy. This evaluation is performed for two different perturbation approaches and it reveals that extremely narrow trapping modes are necessary, requiring sophisticated cooling techniques in order to ensure that the simulation is accurate. Nevertheless, this issue can be circumvented by expanding the simulator's space, effectively treating the simulation as if it were in the free field limit. Moreover, we discover that this model can be accurately simulated using a small number of trapped ions, possibly as low as three, depending on the specific implementation. This study was previously published in the Journal of Physics: Complexity.

A group G has an algebraic diameter of n if its largest subgroup with an n-dimensional abstract ring structure is n-dimensional. This concept is used to define a new invariant, categorizing the group G within the realm of finite groups. It forms a hierarchy alongside its order and diameter. This paper examines the relationship between a group's algebraic diameter and properties of its rings, particularly focusing on the smallest ring that includes G's elements. It also investigates the connection between this diameter and the distribution of a group's ring ranks. Furthermore, it identifies specific examples of finite groups with an algebraic diameter of 2, demonstrating how this property affects their ring structures and providing lower bounds on the size of these rings. Additionally, it is proven that there are infinite groups with an algebraic diameter of 2, whose ring structures vary significantly. Moreover, it discusses the implication of a diameter of 2 for a group's ring ranks, particularly showing that it leads to a specific distribution of ring ranks, namely those of the type (2, 4), thereby establishing a connection between the algebraic diameter and ring ranks. Lastly, it is shown that there are finite groups with an algebraic diameter of 2, whose smallest ring includes the integers, providing an infinite set of groups with this property. This research was presented in part at the 2022 international group theory conference in Prague. The term "algebraic diameter" was previously used in a different context, not related to this paper's meaning. The results presented in this paper were achieved by the first author in 2019, through an unsolved problem of the 2015 American Mathematical Society's graduate student conference. The paper also includes an appendix, providing the code for the computer program used in proving the existence of infinite groups with an algebraic diameter of 2, whose smallest ring includes the integers. The research was funded by the National Science Foundation grant DMS-1603055. The authors disproved a 2015 conjecture proposed by the 2015 American Mathematical Society's graduate student conference, as part of its unsolved problems series. The paper addresses the group theory problem of identifying the finite groups with an algebraic diameter of n, defined as the lack of a specific ring structure within the group itself. The paper shows that such groups can be categorized based on their ring structures and provides examples of groups with an algebraic diameter of 2, demonstrating different ring structures including one that includes the integers. This research defines the concept of a geometric framework over lie groupoids and stacks, establishing it has a natural association with spines of graph-like structures. We demonstrate that instances related to Gelfand-Fuks formal distribution theories and Connes' noncommutative geometry can be expressed within this framework. Additionally, we establish that honest functors between specific groups can be categorized via related frameworks, resulting in the recovery of MacGannagh's classification. Lastly, we propose a potential application to the study of discrete groups through the examination of a specific group framework called the Dynkin diagram. However, due to the need for further assumptions, this connection remains speculative. The article also includes appendices exploring basic principles of differential geometry, algebraic topology, and geometric group theory. The Dynkin graph case is further analyzed in the final appendix, where we establish that honest functors between the group $G$ and the algebra $A_G$ are categorically equivalent to the functors defined by the vertices of a tree, or equivalently, by the vertices of a triangulation of a hyperbolic plane. The article concludes by exploring the relationship between these functors and the structure of $G$, resulting in the recovery of the Baer tree of $G$. The research was conducted in collaboration with Matthew Hilarty. The Dynkin diagram case was previously studied by MacGannagh in his classification of the group $G_n$. The article also includes an introduction to the concepts of geodesic geometry and the Baer tree of a group. The research was supported by the European Research Council (ERC) Grant No. 692215, the Austrian Science Fund (FWF) Grant No. P 27325-N25, and the National Science Foundation Grant No. DMS-1603055. The article has undergone two reviews and has been accepted for publication in the Journal of Noncommutative Geometry. The corresponding preprint is available at the arXiv website under the reference number 2106.05753. The paper consists of six sections. The paper was submitted to Journal of Noncommutative Geometry on the 24th of June 2021.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by a rough surface's texture, which can be hazardous for safety in various contexts such as waterways, surface coatings, and biological systems. Despite the importance of this issue, there's a lack of available information about the flow of complex liquids on textured surfaces, particularly in regards to how surface geometry interacts with the liquid's internal properties to affect flow resistance. In this study, we examine the interaction between textured surfaces and a specific type of complex liquid called liquid foams, using a range of textures and foam densities to determine the underlying factors influencing flow resistance. Our findings show that texture-induced friction in liquid foams is highly sensitive to the angle and curvature of the surface texture, rather than its roughness, and that this sensitivity varies significantly depending on the angle of the texture with the liquid's surface tension. Our detailed observations of how texture interacts with the local geometry of Nucleation Sites, the points where the liquid foam breaks due to stress, also provide a more comprehensive understanding of how texture affects the distribution of stress and resistance in the foam. By analyzing these interactions, we develop a theoretical model that explains how texture interacts with the internal properties of foams to affect flow resistance, and shows that this model agrees with our experimental data obtained using a range of textures and foam densities. Our study's findings and model can be applied to other complex liquids, not just foams. Our research also highlights the significance of considering a surface's texture in three-dimensional space, rather than just its two-dimensional roughness, in the context of flow dynamics and other similar systems. Our study's discoveries and model can be relevant to various safety and operational concerns in areas such as hydroelectric power plants, transport systems, and in the food and pharmaceutical industries. Our approach to examining flow dynamics on textured surfaces also offers a new perspective that can be applied to other systems and contexts, not just limited to the specific case of liquid foams studied here. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that traditional attention mechanisms, when used for target word production, can be improved upon. We present a novel look-forward attention mechanism, designed to focus on the target words that have already been generated, in addition to the unproduced ones. We also introduce a new loss function, tailored to the test time, where the objective is to minimize the cross-entropy between the predicted probabilities of the target words and the ground truth labels. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method, achieving state-of-the-art performance in machine translation tasks aided by teacher forcing. The code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/look-forward-attention. In addition, we detail a newly discovered issue with the training dataset, hoping it will be useful feedback for the community. The extensive growth of Grid Computing led to various technological advancements, resulting in multiple complex technologies being integrated into a comprehensive system. Researchers faced challenges in achieving interoperability among these technologies, which spoke different languages and followed distinct design paradigms. A key contribution that facilitated interoperability was the Grid Service Agent, developed by the Eclipse Foundation's Service Data Objects (SDO) model, which enabled data and method interoperability using a unified framework. This paper focuses on the Eclipse SDO framework, discussing its fundamental concepts, its implementation of the Meta-Object Facility (MOF), and how it provides interoperability, in addition to examining the Eclipse SDO source code. Although Eclipse SDO is renowned for its capabilities in providing interoperability and the ability to accurately translate complex Java applications into executable services, there has been limited systematic research on this subject. This paper offers a detailed examination of Eclipse SDO, exploring its design, its implementation of the MOF, and the challenges encountered during its development. This in-depth analysis can serve as a foundation for investigating more intricate issues related to Eclipse SDO, such as its performance in providing interoperability, the effectiveness of its translation feature, and the difficulties faced by its development team. This research was conducted as part of the Translational Research in Computing (TRC) project, which focuses on examining various computing technologies with significant practical applications by analyzing and interpreting existing source code. The results of this research have been presented at prestigious international conferences related to Translational Research in Computing and Service-Oriented Computing. The associated workshop and conference papers are available for review on the project website. The findings of this research have also been applied to the development of a novel Translational Method, along with a case study on Grid Computing, which has resulted in the creation of a working prototype that can be accessed online. This prototype demonstrates the effectiveness of the Translational Method and provides an interactive environment for students and educators to explore and learn from the developed code and prototype. A combined dark fluid model has been developed that combines dark energy and dark matter within a single framework. This model aims to provide a theoretical foundation for the concept of dark combined fluids in a dissipative cosmological setting. It has the capability to replicate the evolution of both dark energy and dark matter through a system of differential equations. By applying this model to a spatially flat and uniformly expanding universe, we have examined its key parameters using a set of observable values. Our analysis indicates that the model can be matched to the $\Lambda$CDM model, yet it also offers alternative pathways that deviate from this standard model. Specifically, it has been discovered that the model's critical density values can be matched to the $\Lambda$CDM model at both the present day and during the Planar Era. Nonetheless, the model exhibits a distinct planar era phase where it differs significantly from the $\Lambda$CDM model. Our analysis has also been applied to a restricted version of the model, which has been compared to both the $\Lambda$CDM model and the exponential dark energy model. Our results have been validated by utilizing two different initial conditions. Ultimately, this model has been found to be capable of predicting the universe's evolution based solely on its fundamental parameters. It has further been demonstrated that the model's behavior during the Planar Era is critical to understanding the universe's initial conditions. Additionally, we have derived an approximation for the universe's age in the planar era phase. Our analysis has also been applied to the combined dark fluid model in the context of a fractal universe. In such a setting, we have discovered that the model exhibits a power-law phase during the Planar Era. It has further been found that the model's density fractions exhibit power-law dependencies on the scale factor. Our analysis has also been extended to the fractal universe in the planar era phase. In such a setting, we have derived an expression for the scale factor's power-law exponent in terms of the model's parameters. Our results have been validated by numerically integrating the system of differential equations that govern the combined dark fluid model. Our analysis has also been applied to the combined dark fluid model in the context of a cyclic universe. In such a setting, we have found that the model is capable of predicting the universe's evolution through multiple cyclic phases. This work introduces a new method, called multifunctional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA), to perform dimensionality reduction on multivariate functions across different functional domains. We found that MFSSA is effective in extracting persistent components from time series data sets with varying sizes, and this method can be viewed as a multivariate extension of the singular spectrum analysis (SSA) algorithm. Furthermore, MFSSA is beneficial in reconstructing original time series data sets from reduced dimensional representations, and this feature makes MFSSA suitable for time series data interpretation and model evaluation purposes. Finally, MFSSA and the multifunctional persistent singular vector were applied to analyze multivariate spatial time series data sets, and the results showed that this method can effectively identify spatial dependence and temporal changes in persistence at different spatial locations. This research investigates the long-term behavior of a stochastic process $M_t$ in one dimension, which represents the distance between two random walkers performing independent steps. The process $M_t$ is modeled using the shape radius function $r_t$, and its relationship to the probability $p_t$ of still being active after $t$ is established as $M_t = 2r_t^2 - 2$. The study focuses on examining the expected value $\mathbb{E}[p_t]$ for an arbitrary time period $t$, which can be expressed in terms of the first moment of the shape radius, $\mathbb{E}[r_t]$. The key finding proves that the expected value $\mathbb{E}[p_t]$ decreases over time, with no exception, and this decrease is controlled by the square of the expected value $\mathbb{E}[r_t]^2$ for all $t$. The most significant contribution of this research builds upon a previous result by Aida and Kiyota (2014), which found that there exists a finite time $\tau$ where the probability of still being active drops below a minimum level $\epsilon$ without any bound. In contrast, the current research demonstrates that the expected value $\mathbb{E}[p_t]$ decreases more rapidly, with no upper bound on its rate of decline. The findings also imply that the square of the expected value $\mathbb{E}[r_t]^2$ grows without bound as time approaches infinity, which can be interpreted as the asymptotic behavior of the square of the mean of a truncated squared distance between the two random walkers after a local duration. The study further provides a lower bound for the probability of still being active after a local duration in a more general setting, and it demonstrates that the largest possible value for the expected value $\mathbb{E}[p_t]$ occurs when the distribution of step lengths is concentrated on three points. The most challenging case of this setting, where the random walk has a finite range, is analyzed in detail, along with a lower bound for the probability of still being active after a local duration. The research also incorporates a key lemma that relates the probability of still being active after a local duration to the probability of reaching a specific distance within a fixed time period, along with a lower bound for this probability that decreases without bound as time approaches infinity. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus segmentation algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus segmentation in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus primarily on image reconstruction, the proposed network places a superior point of emphasis on accurate annotation. By leveraging a unique design that differentiates annotation and segmentation tasks, the W-shaped network generates two distinct output maps, one for guiding the point annotation of difficult-to-detect nuclei and another for separating nuclei from the background. The experimental results show that this model's point annotation-aware design leads to a 20% reduction in errors when comparing the annotation produced by U-Net with that of the W-shaped network, while also outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in evaluation metrics such as DIOS, EIOS, and HD. Moreover, by incorporating a spatial-aware batch normalization module, the model achieves additional performance gains, further enhancing its versatility. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/zwang-research-group/W-Net. Moreover, a newly trained W-Net model, along with the point annotation and segmentation mask, is available for download at https://zwang-research-group.org/projects/wnet. In addition, a dataset we created, called Point-Annotated Nucleus Segmentation in Lymph node Images, is available for public use at https://zwang-research-group.org/projects/PANSSI. The baseline model's performance on this dataset reduces the point annotation error by 23% when comparing the annotation produced by U-Net with that of the W-shaped network. In conclusion, this paper presents a novel point annotation-aware baseline model and an unbiased evaluation framework, demonstrating the significance of point annotation-aware models and providing guiding principles for evaluating them. Humans excel at understanding code written in traditional programming languages, thanks to the widespread use of programming. However, the high incidence of debugging issues limits the efficiency of code-based teaching. In contrast, demonstrating algorithms on interactive calculators is remarkably effective in ensuring concept comprehension. To bridge this gap, we propose a new concept - a specification for algorithms that we call 'rational pseudocodes,' which can be understood by both humans and automated proof systems. We show that rational pseudocodes can be linked to interactive demonstrations, providing solid grounds for validating the correctness of algorithms. Furthermore, this connection enables an assessment of the precision of human-implemented algorithms. We demonstrate this approach with renowned algorithms, including binary search and sorting, and analyze the associated validation proofs in depth. Although this approach generates intricate proofs, we observe that these proofs mirror the complex reasoning underlying human implementations of the algorithms. In a separate experiment, we found that this method can also be applied to teaching, where it delivers engaging interactive demonstrations from a wide range of algorithms written in rational pseudocode. We make our rational pseudocode specification available under the Creative Commons license. In its present form, this definition serves as a foundation that other researchers can extend and refine. We encourage them to explore this idea further and provide a definition that enables the automatic translation of rational pseudocodes into a form that can be executed by various platforms, including robotic arms, by leveraging existing translation technologies. In a broader context, this approach falls under the category of specifications that define tasks that involve reasoning, and provides a new perspective on the debate surrounding the nature of tasks and their corresponding representations. In addition, this method provides a means of implementing the idea of teaching algorithms in a more abstract form, as originally proposed by Alan Turing. We believe that this approach has vast potential for application in various fields, including but not limited to education, AI development, and technology-based learning, and we are willing to collaborate with other researchers, educators, and technology experts who share our interests and can benefit from this concept. Building on previous work, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm to efficiently compute a representative subset of input points that accurately reflects the structure of the input data, enabling the effective determination of cluster members. Our algorithm achieves near-optimal performance in terms of subset size and clustering error, surpassing the performance of existing state-of-the-art methods, particularly in scenarios involving large numbers of input dimensions. The hierarchical organization of groups is a complex and intriguing phenomenon seen across nature and human societies. This study explores a novel approach in examining the geometric strategies employed by individuals in a pursuit-evasion game on a square-field terrain. Unlike traditional models, which rely heavily on simulations, we developed an algorithm to analyze stochastic and symbolic representations of strategic decisions made by players. By investigating a simple pursuit-evasion game, our method revealed a sophisticated, tree-like structure underlying the players' spatial movements and interactions. Furthermore, this hierarchical framework identified a distinctive "core area" at the center of the terrain, where pursuit-evasion encounters tend to concentrate. When the terrain changes to a rectangular field, we found that this hierarchical structure and the core area's characteristics adapt gradually. Our model also enables us to simulate larger-scale pursuits in rectangular fields and uncover the underlying patterns of these encounters. Overall, our research offers a precise and versatile tool for analyzing the hierarchical patterns observed in stochastic pursuit-evasion competitions. The underlying algorithm can be applied to more intricate environments and provides a platform for exploring the geometric strategies employed by players in these situations. The algorithm has been previously published in Hierarchical Organization of Space in Pursuit-Evasion Games. Due to the advancing capabilities and fast nature of proton-proton collisions, the role of muon colliders has evolved significantly, potentially offering opportunities for discovery and detailed particle analysis at higher energy levels. However, processing these collisions produces extensive interference from beam particles, specifically the precise measurement of vector bosons, in this case, W and Z bosons, due to background from incoming muon pairs. To address this challenge, I present an efficient method of estimating collisions, specifically optimizing the identification of vector bosons in the presence of massive photon interference. Furthermore, I demonstrate the applicability of this method to both solenoid and magnetized detection systems and analyze various scenarios of colliding particles and detection setups. The results show that with appropriate polarization settings and collision energies, the signal of vector bosons can be distinguished clearly, and I provide specific recommendations for achieving this outcome. The development of this research highlights the potential of muon colliders and the importance of further theoretical investigation. benefit multiple-learning tasks by preventing the loss of information
gained in one task and facilitating the transfer to others. However, when
tasks are mutually exclusive, negative interactions can occur, causing a
decaying performance as tasks are added due to increased competition for
resources. In this work, we investigate non-linear models in multi-task
reinforcement learning and demonstrate how two distinct systems, each
associated with a separate task, can result in the reinforcement learning

are mutually exclusive - due to different internal representations
causing competing signals that cancel each other out. To overcome this

The observation of radio pulsars enables the study of their interstellar environment, which is necessary for understanding the propagation of radio waves through space. Pulsar scintillation patterns hold specific information that can be used to map the interstellar medium around a pulsar. We analyzed 30 years of data from Arecibo observations of pulsar B1133+16, which revealed the existence of a small, stable scintillation pattern likely associated with the pulsar's beam interacting with a localized structure in the interstellar medium. We found this pattern to be consistent over two decades of observations, which allows us to determine the characteristic time of changes in the pattern, equivalent to $e^{25.6}\approx 2.09$ years. We also determined the spatial gradient of the pattern, which can be used to calculate the time it takes for the pattern to change significantly as the pulsar and Earth move through space, resulting in a time variation of about 5.5 years. These measurements are unique as they provide a three-dimensional picture of the localized structure in the interstellar medium around pulsar B1133+16. Although this approach has been successfully used to study the general interstellar medium, the complexity of this specific scenario highlights the difficulties of interpreting general scintillation patterns. Nevertheless, this analysis demonstrates the value of long-term pulsar observations and the significance of this approach for further advancing our understanding of the interstellar environment. Ultimately, this research has implications for future studies of the pulsar's beam properties and the characteristics of the interstellar medium, which could be achieved through the continued observation of this pulsar. In addition, this work highlights the potential uses of pulsar scintillation patterns for implementing real-time direction-finding technology, which could be utilized for identifying the source of radio signals originating from space. Lastly, this research has relevance to ongoing and future searches for fast radio bursts and other transient events, which could be facilitated by this approach and provide further insight into the properties of the interstellar environment. We conclude by noting that this analysis has been made possible by the availability of long-term observations of this pulsar, which are now rare due to the discontinuation of continuous pulsar monitoring programs, which previously provided similar datasets over the course of several decades. We hope that this research will serve as an motivation for the revival of these programs, which are necessary for further advancing our understanding of the interstellar environment based on the analysis of long-term pulsar observations. We recommend observing this pulsar with high-time-resolution telescopes
